title: Why Is the Night Sky Dark? (It's Weirder Than You Think)
creator: Field Notes Science
description:
If the universe is full of stars, why isn't the night sky blazing white? The answer to Olbers' paradox tells us the universe had a beginning.

sentences.t: If the universe goes on forever and it's full of stars, then every direction you look should eventually hit a star, so why isn't the night sky blindingly bright?

So, back to the sky.
This question has a name, it's called Olbers' paradox, after a German astronomer named Heinrich Olbers who wrote about it in 1823.
But people were puzzling over it long before him, including Kepler, about two hundred years earlier.
Here's the logic, and stay with me, because it's surprisingly convincing.
Imagine you're standing in the middle of a huge forest.
Close by, you can see the gaps between the trees, but if the forest is big enough, every line of sight eventually ends on a tree trunk.
Now swap trees for stars, and the forest for an infinite universe.
Faraway stars look dimmer, sure, but there are more of them the further out you go, and those two effects cancel out exactly.
So every point in the sky should be as bright as the surface of a star.
Which, obviously, it's not, because you're alive and you can go outside at night.
For a long time, people tried to explain it with dust, like maybe clouds of gas between the stars block the light.
But that doesn't work, because over time, the dust would absorb so much energy that it would heat up and start glowing too.
The real answer has two parts, and both of them are kind of mind-blowing.
Part one, the universe isn't infinitely old.
It's about thirteen point eight billion years old, and light travels at a fixed speed, so there's a limit to how far away we can see.
Beyond that, the light simply hasn't had time to reach us yet.
So the forest isn't endless, at least not the part we can see, and there are gaps where the trees run out.
Part two, the universe is expanding.
As light travels through expanding space, it gets stretched to longer and longer wavelengths, and it loses energy along the way.
Light from the very early universe started out blazing hot, and it's been stretched so much that it now shows up as microwaves.
And that's the cosmic microwave background, the leftover glow from the Big Bang.
So in a sense, the sky is glowing in every direction, it's just glowing in a color your eyes can't see.
Which I think is one of the most beautiful facts in all of science.
The darkness between the stars is actually telling us the universe had a beginning.
Next time, we're going to look at how we actually measured that thirteen point eight billion number.
Thanks for watching, and look up tonight.
